metadata.file_name: 124. Mirazchiyski & Gershteyn (2024). ﻿Technology factors related to the differences in paper and online reading scores in PIRLS 2016.pdf
metadata.title: Technology factors related to the differences in paper and online reading scores in PIRLS 2016

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 paper reading and ePIRLS 2016 electronic reading data from the same grade 4 students in seven European countries, restricting the analytic sample to students who participated in both modes (Ireland removed due to low overlap). PIRLS/ePIRLS employ a complex multistage cluster sampling design (schools sampled with PPS, intact classrooms sampled within schools) and multiple-matrix booklets/tasks, so the authors compute standard errors using the PV-specific procedures. For the student-and-school models, they apply student total weights after merging school characteristics to students; for the teacher model they apply teacher total weights. Because the dependent variable is derived from plausible values (differences between corresponding PVs across modes), analyses are repeated across the five PVs and combined using both sampling weights and replicate weights via the R package RALSA.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes the plausible values (PVs) generation and the required PV-repeated estimation with sampling and replicate weights, but it does not explicitly report a separate missing-data strategy for questionnaire variables (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion or imputation rules). Given that PIRLS/ePIRLS contextual scales are constructed by the IEA study center and the analysis is conducted through RALSA, the authors likely rely on the IDB’s prepared variables and PV framework; however, the manuscript does not document the exact missingness handling for the ICT/background predictors. This is a reporting gap because missingness in predictors can affect regression coefficients and their standard errors.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2016 (paper) and ePIRLS 2016 (electronic) for grade 4 students in European countries that took both modes with the same sample; retained only students who participated in both modes (paper and ePIRLS sessions). Ireland was removed because the overlap between PIRLS and ePIRLS samples was only 53.7% (below the study’s quality threshold). The remaining countries’ overlap was high (average 86.6%, with Denmark as low as 71.4% and Portugal as high as 98.2%), and analyses were conducted at the population level using PV-based score differences rather than individual-level comparisons.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 (ePIRLS 2016) Grade 4 Reading for information (paper vs electronic modes)
main_findings.target_variable: Mode difference in reading achievement (e-reading PV minus paper PV)
top_predictors: Device use in and out school
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression with PV-difference outcomes; model fit reported as country-specific R-squared/adjusted R-squared and F-statistics (e.g., Model 1 R-squared ranges ~0.00–0.02; Model 2 R-squared ranges ~0.01–0.03). No ML metrics (accuracy/AUC/RMSE) reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016/ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading-for-information the study leveraged device use in and out school, computer self-efficacy, home resources for learning, home digital device access, and computers-to-students ratio to explain the mode difference between electronic and paper reading PVs, finding limited and country-specific associations (notably device use and self-efficacy in Portugal; home digital access in Italy; computers-to-students ratio and digital-resource-shortage instruction effects in Denmark/Italy; and home resources for learning predicting differences in several countries). This indicates that technology-related inequalities and school ICT capacity may shape whether electronic reading outperforms paper, but effects are small and not consistent across all European contexts.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PIRLS 2016 paper reading and ePIRLS 2016 electronic reading for grade 4 students in six European countries (Ireland excluded due to low overlap), using the difference between corresponding plausible values (PVs) across modes as the outcome. Because PIRLS/ePIRLS use complex sampling and PVs, the authors repeat computations across five PVs and aggregate standard errors using sampling and replicate weights via RALSA. They fit ordinary least squares (OLS) regressions (multilevel modeling deemed unsuitable due to low between-school variance) and report country-specific R-squared/adjusted R-squared and F-statistics rather than ML performance metrics. Results show statistically significant but small coefficients in a subset of countries: access and use of technology (especially in Italy and Portugal) and student self-efficacy (Portugal and Slovenia) relate to mode differences, while classroom teacher variables show no significant relationships. The study is cross-sectional and does not provide a documented missing-data strategy for predictors beyond the PV framework, so causal claims about technology effects cannot be inferred.
